titre: Hooker Chemical Broke No Law. Congress Legislates Anyway
accroche: In 1953, a chemical company sells a plot of land filled with waste for one dollar; twenty-five years later, the United States declares a federal emergency there.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1894, the industrialist William T. Love has the beginning of a canal dug near Niagara Falls, meant to supply a hydroelectric plant; the financial panic of 1893 dries up investors, and work stops in 1906 after barely a mile of trench. Starting in 1942, the chemical company Hooker Chemical, which buys the site in 1947, buries there about 21,800 short tons (19,800 metric tons) of industrial residues, before stopping in early 1952 and covering the trench with soil. On April 28, 1953, Hooker transfers the land for a symbolic one dollar to the Niagara Falls school board; the deed mentions the buried waste and releases the company from any future liability. A school is built directly on top, a second opens six blocks away the same year, along with eight hundred single-family homes and two hundred forty public housing units. In October and November 1976, articles in the *Niagara Falls Gazette* reveal the presence of chemical substances in the neighborhood; the state multiplies its sampling, and classifies the area as a health threat in the spring of 1978.

## A Company That Did Nothing Illegal

On August 2, 1978, the State of New York declares a health emergency; five days later, President Jimmy Carter announces a federal health emergency and releases emergency funds: the first time in the history of the United States that such funds are mobilized for a disaster other than a natural one. As early as 1979, the federal government brings suit against Hooker Chemical, but on what basis, given that burying industrial waste was subject to no federal law in the 1940s and 1950s? The only federal waste law then in force, passed in 1976, covered only future waste management, not landfills already closed. On December 11, 1980, Congress fills this gap by passing the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act: it creates a federal cleanup fund, financed by a tax on the petrochemical industry, and above all retroactive liability: a polluter can be made to pay today for a release that was perfectly legal at the time it occurred.

## The Shift

It is this last point that changes the very nature of the rule: liability law ordinarily requires fault or illegality at the time of the events. The 1980 law frees itself from that, and adds to it total joint liability among responsible parties: each may be required to pay for the entire cleanup, and then go after the others afterward. This mechanism, nicknamed “Superfund,” has since been used to finance the cleanup of more than a thousand sites in the United States. Love Canal itself, the first site placed on the federal priorities list that the law had just created, was not removed from it until 2004: the law it brought into being took twenty-four more years than its passage to cure it.

repere.texte: Between 1942 and 1952, Hooker Chemical buries about 21,800 short tons (19,800 metric tons) of chemical residues in the abandoned Love Canal, near Niagara Falls, before transferring the land for one dollar in 1953. On August 2, 1978, the State of New York declares a health emergency there; President Carter does the same at the federal level five days later.

carte.punch: A company buried its waste legally. Congress rewrote the law for it anyway.
carte.idee: In 1953, Hooker Chemical transfers for one dollar a plot of land filled with waste since 1942. Schools and houses are built there; a health emergency is declared in 1978. In 1980, Congress invents retroactive liability: paying for a release that was legal at the time.

quiz.question: How does the liability created by the 1980 federal law after Love Canal differ from ordinary civil liability?
choix: It applies only to companies still operating at the time of the trial
It requires proof that the company knew, at the time, that its waste was dangerous
It can apply to a release that was perfectly legal at the time, and make a single responsible party jointly liable for the entire cleanup
It automatically shifts the burden of cleanup to the State, with no recourse against the company
quiz.explication: The 1980 law makes liability retroactive, without requiring fault or illegality at the time of the events, and joint among identified responsible parties: each may have to pay the whole before going after the others.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Hooker Chemical do at the Love Canal site between 1942 and 1952, before transferring the land?
choix: It buried about 21,800 short tons of chemical residues there, then covered the trench with soil
It built a hydroelectric plant there, which was left unfinished
It stored waste there that it then removed entirely before the sale
It buried waste there with the explicit authorization of the school board
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between 1942 and early 1952, Hooker Chemical buries about 21,800 short tons of chemical residues in the abandoned canal, then covers the trench with soil before transferring the land in 1953.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what way is Jimmy Carter's federal emergency declaration of August 7, 1978, a first?
choix: It is the first time an American president personally visits a polluted site
It is the first federal law banning the burial of chemical waste
It is the first time federal emergency funds are mobilized outside a natural disaster
It is the first time an American company is convicted of pollution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Five days after the declaration by the State of New York, Carter announces the federal health emergency: the first time in the history of the United States that federal emergency funds are mobilized for a disaster other than a natural one.
